# skill-author - Agent Context

Project-level context for AI agents working in this repository. It is separate from the skill itself
(`skills/skill-author/SKILL.md`), which holds the task-specific instructions.

## Project Purpose

`skill-author` is an npm package that ships an Agent Skill for creating, validating and publishing other skills, plus a
CLI to install it and to validate any skill. It is itself an example of the patterns it teaches: it must always pass
its own validator.

## Repository Layout

```
skill-author/
  bin/install.js               # CLI: install | validate <dir> (thin wrapper over lib/)
  lib/frontmatter.js           # strict zero-dependency frontmatter parser
  lib/validate.js              # validateSkill(dir), validatePackage(root): return problems, never exit
  lib/install.js               # install(options): copy the skill into harness folders, returns results
  index.js                     # programmatic API (re-exports lib/)
  scripts/validate.js          # `npm run validate`, delegates to the CLI
  scripts/sync-version.js      # npm `version` hook: copies the version into .claude-plugin/plugin.json
  skills/skill-author/
    SKILL.md                   # canonical skill, the primary deliverable
    references/                # frontmatter-spec.md, examples.md, harness-compat.md (loaded on demand)
    assets/SKILL.template.md   # starter template (validated by a test)
  tests/                       # node:test suites, run with `npm test`
  .claude-plugin/              # Claude Code plugin + marketplace manifests
  .github/workflows/           # validate.yml (CI, Node 18-24), publish.yml (npm trusted publishing on release)
```

## Key Invariants

- `SKILL.md` is the single entrypoint of the skill and stays under 500 lines. Long material goes in `references/`,
  templates in `assets/`, deterministic helpers in `scripts/`, linked one level deep with relative paths.
- Frontmatter uses only Agent Skills spec fields: `name`, `description`, `license`, `compatibility`, `metadata`,
  `allowed-tools`. Triggers and excludes are `metadata.triggers` / `metadata.excludes` (semicolon-separated strings).
  The official `skills-ref` validator rejects any other top-level field.
- `name` equals the directory name.
- No runtime npm dependencies; scripts use Node built-ins only. Supported Node: 18+.
- Library code in `lib/` and `index.js` never prints or calls `process.exit`; only `bin/` and `scripts/` do.
- `package.json` and `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` carry the same version (`npm version` syncs them; the validator
  fails on a mismatch). Every release updates `CHANGELOG.md`.
- Every path in `package.json` `files` and `pi.skills` exists (checked by `validatePackage`). The package is also a Pi package (`pi` manifest, `pi-package` keyword): keep skills under `skills/` and runtime dependencies at zero.

## Placement Targets

| Target | Project folder | User folder |
|---|---|---|
| claude | `.claude/skills/skill-author/` | `~/.claude/skills/skill-author/` |
| agents (Codex, Pi, OpenCode, Amp, Cline, Gemini CLI...) | `.agents/skills/skill-author/` | `~/.agents/skills/skill-author/` |
| copilot | `.github/skills/skill-author/` | `~/.copilot/skills/skill-author/` |
| pi (opt-in) | `.pi/skills/skill-author/` | `~/.pi/agent/skills/skill-author/` |
| opencode (opt-in) | `.opencode/skills/skill-author/` | `~/.config/opencode/skills/skill-author/` |
| generic | `skills/misc/skill-author/` | none |

Codex reads `.agents/skills`, not `.codex/skills`. Pi and OpenCode 2 both read `.agents/skills`, so `agents` is the recommended target for them; `pi` and `opencode` are opt-in and kept out of the default set because Pi warns on duplicate skill names. Each target's `reads` list in `lib/install.js` must stay true: re-measure with probe skills before changing it.

## Commands

```bash
npm test                            # all tests (node --test)
npm run validate                    # validate this package's skill and packaging
node bin/install.js validate DIR    # validate any skill directory
node bin/install.js install --dry-run
npm version patch|minor|major       # bump, sync plugin.json, commit, tag
```

## What Agents Should NOT Do

- Do not add external npm dependencies.
- Do not add top-level frontmatter fields outside the spec.
- Do not embed secrets, tokens, or absolute paths in `SKILL.md`.
- Do not make `lib/` functions print or exit.
- Do not edit `.github/workflows/publish.yml` without understanding npm trusted publishing: it authenticates with OIDC
  (`id-token: write`), there is no `NPM_TOKEN` secret. It runs `npm stage publish`, so a release is staged and goes live only
  after a maintainer approves it with 2FA (npmjs.com Staged Packages tab, or `npm stage approve <stage-id>`).
- Do not publish or push tags without being asked.

# Skill Author

## 1. Define the Job

You create, review and publish Agent Skills: folders whose `SKILL.md` tells an agent how to do one job reliably. Success means the skill passes `skill-author validate` and the official spec validator, and an agent can choose it from its description alone.

## 2. Trigger Conditions

- The user asks you to make, write or add a skill for some job.
- The user wants an existing `SKILL.md` reviewed, fixed, shortened or made portable across harnesses.
- The user wants a skill checked against the Agent Skills spec.
- The user wants a skill published, for example as an npm package or a git repository.

## 3. Exclusions

- Installing a skill someone else wrote (use the harness's installer or `npx skills add <owner/repo>`).
- Running or executing skills.
- Writing project documentation such as a README or `AGENTS.md`.
- Anything that needs more than one job in a single skill: split it, or write an orchestrator that routes to the others.

## 4. Workflow Steps

1. Define the single job in at most three sentences: what it does, for whom, and what success looks like. If you find two jobs, make two skills.
2. Check the installed skills for one that already covers the job. If one does, route to it by name instead of copying its content.
3. Create `<skills-dir>/<name>/SKILL.md` from `assets/SKILL.template.md`. The directory name must equal the `name` field.
4. Write the frontmatter using the rules in `references/frontmatter-spec.md`: only spec fields, the trigger condition inside `description`, and the trigger phrases and exclusions as strings under `metadata`.
5. Write the body with the seven sections in this order: Define the Job, Trigger Conditions, Exclusions, Workflow Steps, Domain Conventions, Examples, Validation Checklist.
6. Move long material to `references/`, templates to `assets/` and deterministic helper code to `scripts/`. Link each file with a relative path, one level deep. Keep `SKILL.md` under 500 lines.
7. Validate: run `npx skill-author validate <skill-dir>`. Fix every error and read every warning. When available, also run the official validator: `skills-ref validate <skill-dir>`.
8. Test routing with two prompts: one that should select the skill and one that should not. Adjust the description until both behave.
9. Place the skill for each harness with `npx skill-author install` (see the placement table), or publish it (see the publishing steps). Check how Pi and OpenCode 2 discover and name it in `references/harness-compat.md`.

## 5. Domain Conventions

### Frontmatter

- Allowed top-level fields: `name`, `description`, `license`, `compatibility`, `metadata`, `allowed-tools`. Any other field makes the official validator fail with `Unexpected fields in frontmatter`.
- `name`: 1 to 64 characters, lowercase letters, digits and single hyphens, no leading or trailing hyphen, equal to the directory name.
- `description`: at most 1024 characters. State what the skill does and when to use it, and put the main use case and trigger words first, because hosts shorten descriptions when many skills are installed.
- `metadata` holds string values only. Use `triggers` (at least three phrases) and `excludes` (at least one) as semicolon-separated strings.

### Body

- Write numbered, imperative steps that an agent can follow without asking a human. Avoid "maybe", "if you want" and other open choices.
- One job per skill. Keep every file reference relative to the skill directory.
- Never embed secrets, tokens or absolute user paths. Avoid harness-specific syntax unless it sits in a section named for that harness.

### Placement

| Harness | Project folder | User folder |
|---|---|---|
| Agent Skills standard: Pi, OpenCode 2, Codex, Amp, Cline, Gemini CLI and others | `.agents/skills/<name>/` | `~/.agents/skills/<name>/` |
| Claude Code (OpenCode 2 and Copilot also read it) | `.claude/skills/<name>/` | `~/.claude/skills/<name>/` |
| GitHub Copilot | `.github/skills/<name>/` (also reads `.claude/skills`, `.agents/skills`) | `~/.copilot/skills/<name>/` or `~/.agents/skills/<name>/` |
| Pi, native | `.pi/skills/<name>/` | `~/.pi/agent/skills/<name>/` |
| OpenCode 2, native | `.opencode/skills/<name>/` | `~/.config/opencode/skills/<name>/` |

`.agents/skills` alone reaches Pi, OpenCode 2 and Codex, so prefer it; Codex does not read `.codex/skills`. Pi warns when it finds the same skill name in two folders it reads, and loads project-level skills only after project trust (`pi --approve`), so for Pi prefer `--global`. `npx skill-author install` writes these folders (`--target=agents|claude|copilot|pi|opencode|generic`, `--global`, `--dry-run`). Measured folder-by-folder results, invocation, hiding a skill from automatic selection, and Pi or OpenCode distribution are in `references/harness-compat.md`.

### Publishing

1. Run `npm test`: it runs the tests and validates the package.
2. Add the release notes to `CHANGELOG.md`.
3. Run `npm version patch|minor|major`: it bumps `package.json`, syncs `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` through the `version` script, commits and tags `vX.Y.Z`.
4. Push the commit and tag (`git push --follow-tags`).
5. Create a GitHub Release; the publish workflow publishes to npm with trusted publishing.
6. Confirm the new version on npmjs.com. Every path in the `files` list of `package.json` must exist.

## 6. Examples

**Fixing legacy frontmatter** (the form skill-author 1.0 taught, now rejected by the spec validator):

```yaml
# before
name: my-skill
description: Formats changelogs.
triggers:
  - write a changelog
excludes:
  - release notes for marketing
```

```yaml
# after
name: my-skill
description: Formats changelogs from git history. Use when asked to write or update a changelog.
metadata:
  triggers: "write a changelog; update the changelog; summarize commits for a release; changelog entry"
  excludes: "marketing release notes"
```

More annotated samples are in `references/examples.md`.

## 7. Validation Checklist

- [ ] `name` equals the directory name and follows the naming rules.
- [ ] Only spec frontmatter fields are used; triggers and excludes are `metadata` strings.
- [ ] `description` states the job and the trigger condition and is at most 1024 characters.
- [ ] The body has all seven sections and `SKILL.md` is under 500 lines.
- [ ] Every referenced file exists and is linked one level deep.
- [ ] No secrets and no absolute user paths.
- [ ] `npx skill-author validate <skill-dir>` reports no errors.
- [ ] A prompt that should trigger the skill does, and one that should not does not.

# skill-author

> A meta-skill for creating, validating, and publishing [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io) that work across Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode, GitHub Copilot, and other harnesses. Ships with a validator that checks any skill against the spec.

[![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/skill-author)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/skill-author)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](LICENSE)
[![CI](https://github.com/vijayet1/skill-author/actions/workflows/validate.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/vijayet1/skill-author/actions/workflows/validate.yml)

## What is a skill?

A skill is a folder whose `SKILL.md` tells an AI agent how to do one job reliably. This package ships the `skill-author`
skill, which helps any agent write other skills, plus two tools: an installer and a validator. Zero runtime dependencies,
Node 18+.

## Install

```bash
npm install -g skill-author      # or run without installing: npx skill-author <command>
```

## Commands

### Install the skill

```bash
skill-author                              # every project target
skill-author install --target=agents      # one or more: claude, agents, copilot, generic, pi, opencode
skill-author install --global             # into your home directory instead of the project
skill-author install --dry-run            # show what would be written
```

| Target | Project folder | User folder (`--global`) | Read by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `agents` | `.agents/skills/` | `~/.agents/skills/` | **Pi, OpenCode 2**, Codex, Copilot, Amp, Cline, Gemini CLI and other Agent Skills hosts |
| `claude` | `.claude/skills/` | `~/.claude/skills/` | Claude Code, OpenCode 2, GitHub Copilot |
| `copilot` | `.github/skills/` | `~/.copilot/skills/` | GitHub Copilot |
| `generic` | `skills/misc/` | none | your own tooling |
| `pi` *(opt-in)* | `.pi/skills/` | `~/.pi/agent/skills/` | Pi only |
| `opencode` *(opt-in)* | `.opencode/skills/` | `~/.config/opencode/skills/` | OpenCode 2 only |

Plain `skill-author` installs the first four. `pi` and `opencode` are opt-in because `agents` already reaches both
harnesses, and installing the same skill into two folders Pi reads makes Pi warn about duplicate skill names (the
installer tells you when you ask for that).

`openai` and `codex` still work as aliases for `agents`. Version 1.0 wrote them to `.codex/skills/`, which Codex does not
read; it loads project skills from `.agents/skills`.

### Pi and OpenCode 2

Folder support below was measured on Pi 1.2.0 and OpenCode 2.0.30 with probe skills, not just read from docs.

**Pi**
```bash
skill-author install --global --target=agents   # user-level: loads with no trust prompt
pi install npm:skill-author                      # or as a Pi package (the npm package declares "pi": { "skills": [...] })
pi -e npm:skill-author                           # try it for one run without changing settings
```
Project-level skills load only after Pi's project trust (accept the prompt or `pi --approve`). Use the skill with
`/skill:skill-author <request>`; run `/reload` after editing.

**OpenCode 2**
```bash
skill-author install --target=agents            # or --target=opencode for .opencode/skills only
```
Or reference the package without copying files, in `opencode.json`:
`"skills": ["./node_modules/skill-author/skills"]`. Load it with `@skill-author` or let the model use the `skill` tool.

Hiding a skill from automatic selection: in OpenCode use `metadata: { opencode/autoinvoke: "false" }` (spec-valid); the
top-level `disable-model-invocation: true` that both Pi and OpenCode honour is not part of the spec, so validate
such skills with `skill-author validate --allow-field=disable-model-invocation <dir>`. Details:
[`references/harness-compat.md`](skills/skill-author/references/harness-compat.md).

### Validate any skill

```bash
skill-author validate path/to/my-skill [more dirs...]
skill-author validate --allow-field=disable-model-invocation path/to/skill   # accept a harness-specific field
skill-author validate                      # this package's own skill and packaging
```

Checks the Agent Skills spec (allowed frontmatter fields, name and description limits, name equals directory), then
skill-author's authoring rules: under 500 lines, the seven body sections, at least three triggers and one exclude, no
secrets, no absolute user paths, every referenced file exists. Exit status is 1 when there are errors, so it works in CI.
For a second opinion use the official reference validator: `skills-ref validate path/to/my-skill`.

### Programmatic API

```js
const skillAuthor = require('skill-author');

skillAuthor.skillPath;                         // absolute path to the canonical SKILL.md
skillAuthor.validate();                        // validate this package's skill -> [{ level, message }]
skillAuthor.validateSkill('path/to/skill');    // validate any skill directory
skillAuthor.install({ target: 'agents', dryRun: true }); // -> [{ target, dir, status }]
```

Nothing in the API prints or exits the process; functions return data.

## Frontmatter

Only fields defined by the specification are valid: `name`, `description`, `license`, `compatibility`, `metadata`,
`allowed-tools`. The official validator rejects anything else, so trigger phrases and exclusions go under `metadata` as
semicolon-separated strings, and the "use when" condition belongs in the `description`:

```yaml
---
name: my-skill
description: Formats changelogs from git history. Use when asked to write or update a changelog.
metadata:
  triggers: "write a changelog; update the changelog; summarize commits for a release"
  excludes: "marketing release notes"
---
```

Skill-author 1.0 taught top-level `triggers:` and `excludes:`; those fail spec validation. See
[`references/frontmatter-spec.md`](skills/skill-author/references/frontmatter-spec.md) and the starter
[`assets/SKILL.template.md`](skills/skill-author/assets/SKILL.template.md).

## Release workflow

```bash
npm test                         # tests + validation
npm version patch                # or minor | major: bumps package.json AND .claude-plugin/plugin.json, commits, tags
git push --follow-tags
```

Add the release notes to `CHANGELOG.md` before running `npm version`, then create a GitHub Release; the publish workflow
stages the release on npm with trusted publishing (OIDC). Approve it with 2FA on npmjs.com (Staged Packages) or
`npm stage approve <stage-id>` and it goes live.

See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md).

## Security

See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

# Annotated examples

Both examples pass `npx skill-author validate` and the official `skills-ref validate`.

## A focused skill

```markdown
---
name: changelog-entry
description: Writes a Keep a Changelog entry from the commits since the last tag. Use when asked to add, draft or update a changelog entry for a release.
metadata:
  triggers: "write a changelog entry; update the changelog; summarize commits for a release; draft release notes"
  excludes: "marketing release announcements; deciding the version number"
---
```

Why it works:

- The description says what it does first, then `Use when` with the situations that should select it.
- The three-plus triggers read like things a person would actually type.
- The exclusions name the nearby jobs it must not take over.

## An orchestrator skill

An orchestrator does one job: choose and sequence other skills. Route to installed skills by name, give each a
fallback when it is missing, and keep tool-specific detail in `references/`.

```markdown
---
name: python-dev
description: Orchestrates Python development - detects the project's real tooling, routes the task to the right workflow skill, and requires the project's own checks to pass. Use when implementing, fixing, refactoring or finishing a change in a Python repository.
metadata:
  triggers: "implement a python feature; fix a python bug; failing pytest or unittest; add a python dependency"
  excludes: "repositories with no Python project files; writing a new skill"
---
```

Why it works:

- It never hard-codes tools; a helper script in `scripts/` reports what the repository actually uses.
- Its workflow table names skills such as `test-driven-development`, and `references/` holds a short inline fallback for machines that lack them.

## Converting a 1.0-style skill

Move top-level `triggers:` and `excludes:` lists into `metadata` as semicolon-separated strings, make sure the
description contains `Use when ...`, and run `npx skill-author validate <dir>`. The rules are in `frontmatter-spec.md`.

# Frontmatter reference

Source of truth: the Agent Skills specification, https://agentskills.io/specification. The reference validator is
`skills-ref` (https://github.com/agentskills/agentskills/tree/main/skills-ref); `npx skill-author validate` applies the
same rules plus skill-author's authoring rules.

## Fields

| Field | Required | Constraints |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | yes | 1-64 characters; lowercase letters, digits and single hyphens; no leading or trailing hyphen; equals the directory name |
| `description` | yes | 1-1024 characters; what the skill does and when to use it |
| `license` | no | License name, or the name of a bundled license file |
| `compatibility` | no | At most 500 characters; environment requirements (products, packages, network) |
| `metadata` | no | Mapping of string keys to string values; for anything the spec does not define |
| `allowed-tools` | no | Space-separated pre-approved tools (experimental; support varies by harness) |

Any other top-level field is an error in the reference validator: `Unexpected fields in frontmatter: ...`.

## What skill-author adds on top

- `description` must contain a trigger condition such as "Use when ...".
- `metadata.triggers`: at least three phrases, separated by semicolons.
- `metadata.excludes`: at least one entry, separated by semicolons.

These live in `metadata` because top-level `triggers:` and `excludes:` (taught by skill-author 1.0) are not part of the
specification and fail validation.

## Supported YAML

The validator accepts a deliberately small subset so a skill never depends on a harness's lenient parser:

- `key: value` with a plain or quoted string value
- `key:` followed by indented `sub: value` lines (a map of strings)
- `# comments` and blank lines

Rejected: tabs, flow sequences (`[a, b]`), block scalars (`>` and `|`), anchors and tags. Quote any value that contains
a colon followed by a space, or that starts with a special character.

## Good and poor descriptions

- Poor: `Helps with PDFs.` (no trigger condition, nothing to match on)
- Good: `Extracts text and tables from PDF files and fills PDF forms. Use when the user mentions PDFs, forms or document extraction.`

Front-load the main use case and its trigger words: hosts such as Codex shorten descriptions first when many skills are installed.

## Size and loading

Hosts load only `name` and `description` at startup, the full `SKILL.md` when the skill is chosen, and `references/`,
`assets/` and `scripts/` files on demand. Keep `SKILL.md` under 500 lines (about 5000 tokens) and link supporting files
one level deep from the skill root.

## Harness-specific optional fields

Some harnesses honour fields the specification does not define. Strict validators (including `skills-ref`) reject
unknown top-level fields, so prefer `metadata` when the harness allows it:

| Goal | Where | Harness |
|---|---|---|
| Hide from automatic selection | `metadata: { opencode/autoinvoke: "false" }` (spec-valid) | OpenCode 2 |
| Hide from automatic selection | top-level `disable-model-invocation: true` (not in the spec) | Pi, OpenCode 2 |

`skill-author validate` accepts namespaced `metadata` keys such as `opencode/autoinvoke` and checks they are
`"true"` or `"false"`. For the top-level form, opt in explicitly:
`skill-author validate --allow-field=disable-model-invocation <dir>`. See `harness-compat.md` for the rest.

# Harness compatibility: Pi and OpenCode 2 (plus the others)

Facts here were **measured** with probe skills on Pi 1.2.0 and OpenCode 2.0.30 (a skill planted in each candidate
folder, then asked which skills the harness could see), and checked against each harness's docs:
pi.dev/docs, opencode.ai/v2/docs/skills, developers.openai.com/codex/skills, docs.github.com (about agent skills).

## Which folders each harness reads

| Folder | Pi | OpenCode 2 | Codex | GitHub Copilot | Claude Code |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `.agents/skills` | yes | yes | yes | yes | no |
| `~/.agents/skills` | yes | yes | yes | yes | no |
| `.claude/skills`, `~/.claude/skills` | no | yes | no | yes | yes |
| `.pi/skills`, `~/.pi/agent/skills` | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `.opencode/skills`, `~/.config/opencode/skills` | no | yes | no | no | no |
| `.github/skills`, `~/.copilot/skills` | no | no | no | yes | no |

`.agents/skills` is the one folder that reaches Pi, OpenCode and Codex together. Prefer it. Add the native folders
only when you want a single-harness install (`skill-author install --target=pi` or `--target=opencode`).

## Pi

- Project-level skills (`.pi/skills`, `.agents/skills`) load only after **project trust**: accept Pi's prompt or run
  `pi --approve`. User-level folders need no trust, so `skill-author install --global` is the smoothest install.
- Name collisions keep the first skill found and print a warning. Installing the same skill into two folders Pi reads
  (for example `agents` and `pi`) triggers it; `skill-author install` warns before you do.
- Invoke explicitly with `/skill:<name> <request>`. Run `/reload` after editing a `SKILL.md`.
- Optional top-level field `disable-model-invocation: true` hides a skill from automatic selection. It is not in the
  spec, so strict validators reject it; run `skill-author validate --allow-field=disable-model-invocation <dir>`.
- Distribute as a Pi package: `pi install npm:<package>`, `pi install git:github.com/<owner>/<repo>` or a local path.
  Either keep skills in a conventional `skills/` folder or declare `"pi": { "skills": ["./skills"] }` in
  `package.json`, and add the `pi-package` keyword to appear in the package gallery. `pi -e <path-or-source>` tries a
  package for one run without touching settings.

## OpenCode 2

- The skill ID comes from the **path** (`<source>/<id>/SKILL.md`), is case-sensitive, and the frontmatter `name` is
  only a display label. Keep the directory lowercase kebab-case and equal to `name`.
- A skill without a `description` is not advertised to the model.
- Duplicate IDs are not warnings: the later source wins (built-ins, `.claude`, `.agents`, `~/.config/opencode`,
  project `.opencode`, then explicit `skills` entries).
- The model loads a skill with the `skill` tool; you load one by mentioning `@<id>` in a prompt.
- Hide a skill from the model with `metadata: { opencode/autoinvoke: "false" }`. This is spec-valid (`metadata` is
  free-form) and passes `skill-author validate`; `disable-model-invocation: true` also works but needs
  `--allow-field`.
- Add extra sources without copying files: `"skills": ["./node_modules/skill-author/skills"]` in `opencode.json`
  (relative paths resolve from the working directory; `~/` and absolute paths work; `https://` URLs load a catalog
  made of an `index.json`).
- Control access with `permissions` entries whose action is `skill` and whose resource is the skill ID.

## Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot

- Claude Code reads `.claude/skills` and `~/.claude/skills`. Claude plugins are described by
  `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`; this package ships one.
- Codex scans `.agents/skills` from the working directory up to the repository root, plus `~/.agents/skills`; it does
  not read `.codex/skills`.
- GitHub Copilot reads `.github/skills`, `.claude/skills` and `.agents/skills` in a project and `~/.copilot/skills` or
  `~/.agents/skills` for you.
